<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{maintheorem} 
	If ZFC is consistent then so is the theory ZF+DC+BPI+there is no Vitali set.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
$\mathbb{E}_0$ is the equivalence relation on $2^\omega$ connecting two binary sequences if they agree on all but finitely many positions.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
The \emph{$\mathbb{E}_0$}-forcing is the poset of all Borel subsets of $2^\omega$ modulo the $\sigma$-ideal generated by Borel partial $\mathbb{E}_0$-selectors, ordered by inclusion. Its generic object will be viewed as a function in $2^\omega$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
$\mathbb{P}$ is the countable support product of $\omega_2$ many copies of the $\mathbb{E}_0$-forcing. Its generic object will be viewed as a function $c\colon \omega_2\times\omega\to 2$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{maindefinition} 
	Let $\langle \mathbb{B}_n\colon n\in\omega\rangle$ be a sequence of complete Boolean algebras such that for every $n\in\omega$, $\mathbb{B}_{n+1}$ is a complete subalgebra of $\mathbb{B}_n$. Let $G\subset\mathbb{B}_0$ be a generic filter. The \emph{associated intersection model} $M$ is the model $\bigcap_n V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_n]$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\textnormal{\cite[Theorem 4.2.9]{z:geometric}} The intersection model is a transitive model of ZF.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The model $M$ is an intersection of countably many transitive classes containing all ordinals, so it is transitive and contains all ordinals. For the same reason, it is closed under G{\" o}del functions. It is also universal in the sense that for every subset $a\subset M$ there is a set $b\in M$ such that $a\subseteq b$ holds: this occurs because for every ordinal $\lambda$, the set $b_\lambda$ of all elements of $M$ of set theoretic rank smaller than $\lambda$ belongs to $V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_n]$, so $b_\lambda\in M$ as desired. By \cite[Theorem 13.9]{jech:newset}, $M$ is a model of ZF.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{dcproposition} 
	\textnormal{\cite[Electronic supplement]{z:geometric}} 
	The intersection model satisfies DC.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $\langle R, \leq\rangle$ be a partial order in the intersection model without minimal elements; I must produce an infinite descending sequence in the intersection model. 
 
 Let $\preceq$ in $V$ be a well-ordering of a large part of the ground model. By recursion on $n\in\omega$ build a descending sequence $\langle r_n\colon n\in\omega\rangle$ of conditions in $R$ in the following way: $r_0\in R$ is arbitrary, and for each $n\in\omega$, $r_{n+1}=\sigma_{n+1}/G$ where $\tau_{n+1}$ is the $\preceq$-least $\mathbb{B}_{n+1}$-name such that $\tau_{n+1}/G< r_n$. Note that for each $m\in\omega$, the sequence $\langle r_n\colon n\geq m\rangle$ can be recovered by the same recursion process in $V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_m]$ starting from $r_m$. It follows that the descending sequence $\langle r_n\colon n\in\omega\rangle$ belongs to the intersection model as required.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
The intersection model $M$ is equal to $V(a)[b]$ where 
	 
	\begin{enumerate} 
		\item $a=\mathbb{B}_0^\omega\cap M$; 
		\item $b=\{\bar p\in a\colon \forall^\infty n\in\omega\ \bar p(n)\in\mathbb{B}_n\cap G\}$. 
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
It is quite clear that $a, b\in M$, so $V(a)[b]\subseteq M$ holds. For the opposite inclusion, first show that $V(a)$ contains all $\omega$-sequences of elements of the ground model which belong to $M$. The reason is that the range of any such sequence $f$ is covered by a set $c$ of cardinality $|\mathbb{B}_0|$ in the ground model, and then $f\in c^\omega$ is in fact a composition of a ground model bijection between $c$ and $\mathbb{B}$ with some element of $\mathbb{B}^\omega\cap M$. 
	 
	For a formula $\phi$ of the $\mathbb{B}_n$-language in the ground model, write $|\phi|_n$ for its Boolean value. In $V(a)[b]$, consider the class $C$ of all $\omega$-sequences $\bar\sigma$ such that for each $n\in\omega$, $\bar\sigma(n)$ is a ground model $\mathbb{B}_n$-name, and $\langle |\bar \sigma(n)=\bar\sigma(n+1)|_n\colon n\in\omega\rangle\in b$ holds. 
	 
	Consider also the binary relations $\approx$ and $\varepsilon$ on $C$ defined by  
	 
	\begin{itemize} 
		\item $\bar\sigma\approx\bar\tau$ if $\langle |\bar\sigma(n)=\bar\tau(n)|_n\colon n\in\omega\rangle\in b$ holds; 
		\item $\bar\sigma\varepsilon\bar\tau$ if $\langle |\bar\sigma(n)\in\bar\tau(n)|_n\colon n\in\omega\rangle\in b$ holds. 
	\end{itemize} 
	 
	\noindent It is not difficult to see that $\approx$ is an equivalence relation ($G\subset\mathbb{B}_0$ is a filter, after all) and $\varepsilon$ respects the equivalence relation $\approx$ (for the same reason). Now, in $V[G]$, consider the class map $\pi$ with domain $C/\approx$ defined by $\pi([\bar\sigma]_\approx)=$the eventual value of $\bar\sigma(n)/G$. The definition of $\approx$ shows that the values of $\pi$ do not depend on the choice of representatives of equivalence classes. Similarly, the map $\pi$ transports $\varepsilon$ to $\in$. It is immediately clear from the definition of the class $C$ that the values of $\pi$ belong to the intersection model. Also, every set $x\in M_\omega$ is in the range of $\pi$. To see this, consider the function $\bar \sigma$ defined by $\bar\sigma(n)=$the first $\mathbb{B}_n$-name such that $\bar\sigma(n)/G=x$ in some fixed well-ordering of a large part of the ground model. The sequence $\bar\sigma$ belongs to $M$ since for every $n\in\omega$, $\bar\sigma\restriction [n, \omega)\in V[G\cap \mathbb{B}_n]$ holds. The sequence $\bar\sigma$ then belongs to $V(a)$ by the first paragraph of the present proof. So, it belongs to $C$, and $\pi(\bar\sigma)=x$ by the definitions. 
	 
	Now, it follows that $\varepsilon$ is a set-like, extensional, and well-founded relation on the class $C/\approx$, since it is isomorphic to one. By the Mostowski collapse lemma applied in the model $V(a)[b]$, it has a unique transitive collapse. This collapse must then be $\pi$. So $\pi$ is a class in $V(a)[b]$ and its range $M$ is a subset of $V(a)[b]$ as desired.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
If the poset $\mathbb{B}_0$ is proper, then in the intersection model every set can be injected into the product of an ordinal with the quotient $\mathbb{E}_0$ space.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $A\in M$ be a set. Let $\preceq$ in $V$ be a well-ordering of a large fragment of the ground model. Let $f$ be the function with domain $A$ which assigns to any element $a\in A$ the set of all sequences $\bar\sigma\in M$ such that for all but finitely many $n$, $\bar\sigma(n)$ is the $\preceq$-first $\mathbb{B}_n$-name in the ground model such that $\bar\sigma(n)/G=a$. It is clear that this function belongs to the model $V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_n]$ for every $n\in\omega$, so it belongs to the intersection model. 
	 
	Now, the properness of $\mathbb{B}_0$ implies that in $V[G]$, every countable subset of the ground model is a subset of a ground model set which is countable there. Thus, in $M$ one can form a function $g$ with domain $A$ such that for every $a\in A$, $g(a)$ is the $\preceq$-first set countable in $V$ which contains a tail of values of the sequences in $f(a)$. Now, let $h$ be the function with domain $A$ which assigns to each $a\in A$ the pair $\langle g(a), u\rangle$ where $u$ is the $\mathbb{E}_0$-class in $\omega^\omega$ which is mapped to the set $g(a)\cap h(a)^\omega$ by the $\preceq$-first bijection between $\omega$ and $g(a)$. It is immediate that $h$ is an injection of $A$ into the product of a subset of the ground model (which is well-orderable) and the $\mathbb{E}_0$ space.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
If the poset $\mathbb{B}_0$ is proper and bounding, then in the intersection model, every set of nonempty sets admits a multi-selector with countable values.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
First use the proper and bounding assumption to show that in the model $V[G]$, for every countable sequence $\bar s$ of ground model sets there is a ground model sequence $\bar t$ of finite sets such that $\forall n\ \bar s(n)\in\bar t(n)$. 
	 
	Now, suppose that $A\in M$ is a set of nonempty sets. Consider the function $f$ with domain $A$ such that for every $a\in A$, the functional value $f(a)$ is a sequence $\bar t$ in the ground model which takes only finite values, such that for all but finitely many $n\in\omega$, $\bar t(n)$ contains a $\mathbb{B}_n$-name $\sigma$ such that $\sigma/G\in A$, and such a sequence $\bar t$ is selected first in some fixed well-ordering of a large part of the ground model. 
	 
	Observe that the function $f$ is well-defined. If $a\in A$ is any element and $x\in a$ is arbitrary, in $V[G]$ one can find a sequence $\bar s$ such that for every $n\in\omega$, $\bar s(n)$ is a $\mathbb{B}_n$-name in the ground model such that $\bar s(n)/G=x$. Then one can approximate $\bar s$ with $\bar t$ in the ground model as indicated in the first paragraph of the present proof, showing that the definition of $f$ minimizes over a nonempty set. 
	 
	Now, let $g$ be the function on $A$ defined by $g(a)=\{x\in a\colon$ for all but finitely many $n\in\omega$ there is an element $\sigma\in f(a)(n)$ which is a $\mathbb{B}_n$-name and $\sigma/G=x\}$. It is immediate that the function $g$ is defined in the same way in every model $V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_n]$, so it belongs to the intersection model. By the definition of $f$, for each $a\in A$, $g(a)\subset a$ is a nonempty set. I must argue that the set $g(a)$ is countable in the intersection model. 
	 
	In order to do that, fix the set $a\in A$. Consider the sequence $\bar u$ defined by $\bar u(n)=\{x\in a\colon$ for every $m\geq n$ there is $\sigma\in f(a)(n)$ which is a ground model $\mathbb{B}_n$-name and $\sigma/B_n=x\}$. The sequence $\bar u$ consists of finite subsets of $g(a)$, and $g(a)$ is the increasing union $\bigcup_n\bar u(n)$. In addition, for each $n\in\omega$ the tail $\bar u\restriction [n, \omega)$ belongs to $V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_n]$, so $\bar u$ belongs to the intersection model. It follows that in $M$, $g(a)$ is an increasing union of finite sets, and by DC in $M$ it follows that such sets are countable.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{bpiproposition} 
 Suppose that $\mathbb{B}_0$ preserves a nonprincipal ultrafilter on $\omega$. Then BPI holds in the intersection model.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $C$ be a Boolean algebra in the intersection model; I must find an ultrafilter on $C$ in the intersection model. As in Proposition~\ref{dcproposition}, I construct  a sequence $\langle F_n\colon n\in\omega\rangle$ of ultrafilters on $C$ such that for every $m\in\omega$, $\langle F_n\colon n\geq m\rangle\in V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_m]$ holds. 
	 
	This is easy to do. Let $\preceq$ in $V$ be a well-ordering of a large part of the ground model. For each $n\in\omega$, write $F_n=\tau_n/G$ for the $\preceq$-first $\mathbb{B}_n$-name $\tau_n$ such that $\tau_n/G$ is an ultrafilter on $C$. Note that the sequence $\langle F_n\colon n\in\omega\rangle$ is as required. 
	 
	Now, let $U\in V$ be a nonprincipal ultrafilter on $\omega$ which generates an ultrafilter in $V[G]$; by an abuse of notation, let $U$ also denote the ultrafilter generated by $U$ in $V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_n]$ for $n\in\omega$. Let $F=\{b\in B\colon\{n\in\omega\colon b\in F_n\}\in U\}$. Clearly, this is an ultrafilter on $C$; I must prove that for every $m\in\omega$, $F\in V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_m]$. This is immediate though. $F$ is recovered in $V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_m]$ as $F=\{b\in B\colon\{n\geq m\colon b\in F_n\}\in U\}$, using the fact that both $U$ and $\langle F_n\colon n\geq m\rangle$ belong to $V[G\cap\mathbb{B}_m]$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
An $\mathbb{E}_0$-tree is an ever-branching tree $T\subset 2^{<\omega}$ such that for every splitnode $t\in T$ and every $u\in T$ extending $t$, the node obtaining from $u$ by flipping its $|t|$-th entry is in $T$ as well.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- fact-1: body_md -->
\label{ufact} 
Let $U$ be a Ramsey ultrafilter on $\omega$. Let $\mathbb{P}$ be a countable support product of any number of $\mathbb{E}_0$-forcings. In the $\mathbb{P}$-extension, $U$ still generates an ultrafilter.
<!-- end fact-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
This is a concatenation of several arguments well-known from pre-existing literature; I will only provide an outline of the proof. Suppose that $p\in\mathbb{P}$ is a condition and $p\Vdash\sigma\subset\omega$ is a set. I must show that there is a condition $r\leq p$ and a set $a\in U$ such that $r\Vdash\check a\subseteq\sigma$ or $r\Vdash\check a\cap\sigma=0$.  
	 
	Let $I$ denote the index set for the product $\mathbb{P}$. A standard fusion argument provides a strengthening $q\leq p$ and a countable set $J\subset I$ such that below $q$, $\sigma$ is in fact a name in the product $\mathbb{Q}$ of $J$-many copies of the $\mathbb{E}_0$-forcing. The poset $\mathbb{Q}$ adds no independent reals by \cite[Example 1.10]{z:subadditive}; so the set $A=\{a\subset\omega\colon\exists r\leq q\ r\Vdash\check a\subseteq\sigma$ or $r\Vdash\check a\cap\sigma=0\}$ is dense in the algebra $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ modulo finite. Use the continuous reading of names to strengthen $q$ if necessary to make sure that the set $A\subset\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ is analytic. Every Ramsey ultrafilter has a nonempty intersection with every analytic set dense in $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ modulo finite by the arguments of \cite{mathias:happy}. This provides the desired condition $r$ and the set $a\in U$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Suppose that $n\in\omega$ is a number.  
	 
	\begin{enumerate} 
		\item For a function $c\colon \omega_2\times\omega\to 2$, the function $c|n\colon\omega_2\times\omega\to 2$ is defined by $(c|n)(\alpha, m)=c(\alpha, n+m)$. 
		\item For a condition $p\in\mathbb{P}$ and a function $v\colon\omega\to 2^n$ such that for every $\alpha\in\omega_2$, $v(\alpha)\in p(\alpha)$ holds, write $p|v$ for the condition defined by the demand $w\in (p|v)(\alpha)$ iff $v(\alpha)^\smallfrown w\in p(\alpha)$. 
		\item For a condition $p\in\mathbb{P}$ and a function $v\colon\mathrm{supp}(p)\to\alpha$, write $p||v$ for the condition in $\mathbb{P}$ with the same domain defined by the demand $w\in (p||v)(\alpha)$ iff $w$ is an initial segment of $v(\alpha)$ or there is $u\in p(\alpha)$ such that $w=v(\alpha)^u$. 
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
Let $n\in\omega$ be a number. The poset $\mathbb{P}$ forces the function $\dot c|n$ to be $\mathbb{P}$-generic over the ground model.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Consider the set $D$ of all conditions $p$ such that for every $\alpha\in\mathrm{supp}(p)$, the stem of $p(\alpha)$ is longer than $n$. It is obvious that the set $D\subset P$ is dense. Let $\pi\colon D\to\mathbb{P}$ be the function defined by $\pi(p)=p|v$ for some (any) function $v\colon \omega_2\to 2^n$ such that for every $\alpha\in\mathrm{supp}(p)$, $v(\alpha)\in p(\alpha)$. It is not difficult to check that $\mathbb{P}$ forces the $\pi$-image of $D\cap\dot G$ to be a generic filter on $\mathbb{P}$ which yields the function $\dot c|n$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
